newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Democrats discuss draft election law.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Democrats discuss draft election law.

text.p: Albania's main political party met on Saturday to discuss a draft of a new electoral law the government must agree in two days time to keep an agreement on early elections on track.
"We are working fast to prepare our draft before Monday," Tritan Shehu, the leader of President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party, told Reuters.
Albania's 10 top political parties signed a "political contract" on Friday committing themselves to holding elections by the end of June in a deal brokered by European envoy Franz Vranitzky.
Vranitzky, on his fourth visit to Albania since popular anger over the collapse of pyramid savings pushed the Balkan nation to the brink of anarchy in March, hailed the contract as a breakthrough.

Under the contract, the 10 parties must agree on a new law on the form of the election by Monday. Nine of the 10 are members of the National Reconciliation Government set up in March. The tenth supports the government from outside.

A dispute between Berisha's Democrats and the Socialists of interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino over the number of seats to be chosen by proportional representation had blocked progress on the election.
The Democrats had been pushing for more seats to be chosen by majority, while the Socialists and other parties in the government wanted more elected by proportional representation.
The contract stipulated that a compromise using both electoral methods would be agreed.
Fino left for a five-day visit to the United States early on Saturday with his finance, justice and foreign ministers.

Fino's spokesman said before he left that a cabinet meeting late on Friday night had adopted a draft electoral law which would be submitted to the 10 signatories of the contract on Monday for their approval.
While the spokesman said the draft could be amended, it was clear that disagreements remained despite the Vranitzky deal.

"The government election draft law seemed to me a very hasty action because it was only yesterday that a consensus among the political parties on the form of the electoral law was achieved," Democratic leader Shehu said.
"The government should not undertake something that was not envisaged in the contract. This is a problem to be resolved by the political parties, the parliament," he said.
Fatos Nano, a former prime minister and the leader of the Socialist party, could not be reached for comment on Saturday.
The Albanian parliament, where the Democrats have an overwhelming 122 out of 140 seats, must approve the new electoral law by next Thursday, May 15, to keep the contract on track for a June 29 vote.
Under Albanian law, the president must issue a decree calling an election at least 45 days before the vote takes place.
Another serious obstacle looms for the political contract in the form of the Salvation Committees, the citizens' groups set up in southern Albania to restore order after the riots.

Berisha's Democrats maintained the committees were the armed wing of the Socialists, and were an obstacle to free elections. The Socialists denied they had anything to do with the committees, and agreed they should disband.
The committees, which blame Berisha for the pyramids fiasco, demand that he resigns and that investors get their money back. Southern residents say their influence is on the wane.
The contract stipulates that the committees should be disbanded 46 days before the election takes place -- next Wednesday, May 14 if the vote is to be held on June 29.
Vranitzky was vague about how the groups were to disband -- "it will be a joint effort," he said -- and who would certify that the disbandment had taken place.
But the groups themselves threw a serious spanner in the works on Saturday by announcing they would meet on May 16 in the southern port city of Vlore to decide on their future.
